Chapter 4: The Power of Updating and Learning from Feedback
Let’s dive into something at the heart of great forecasting—learning to update and adapt as new information comes in.
See, making an accurate prediction isn’t just a one-and-done event. It’s an ongoing journey, where you’re constantly learning and adjusting your course.
In forecasting, the only thing you can really count on is change. There’s always new data, shifting events, or evolving circumstances that can upend yesterday’s assumptions.
Superforecasters aren’t remarkable because they get everything right the first time—they stand out because they’re willing to change their minds as the world changes around them.
This habit of updating is rooted in a concept called “belief revision.” Instead of clinging to their first guess, superforecasters treat every prediction as a work in progress. They’re always on the lookout for fresh information, and they’re ready to adjust their probabilities when the evidence calls for it.
Think of it like a sailor using the stars to navigate. At first, you set a course based on the best info you have. But as the winds shift and currents change, you make small tweaks to stay on track. That’s exactly how top forecasters operate—they’re prepared to change direction when the facts demand it.
So, what habits help them do this well?
First, there’s regular review. Superforecasters don’t just set a prediction and forget about it. They check back at set intervals, asking, “Has anything important changed?”
Second, they make incremental adjustments. Instead of swinging wildly from one extreme to another, they nudge their estimates up or down in small, thoughtful steps—each one backed by the latest evidence.
Third, they track their accuracy. By keeping records of past predictions and comparing them to what actually happened, they can spot patterns—maybe they’re often too optimistic, or perhaps they tend to miss rare events.
And when they do get it wrong—they lean in and learn. They ask, “What went off track? Did I rely on the wrong base rate? Was there a critical detail I missed?” This kind of honest self-examination is how their judgment gets sharper over time.
Feedback is the fuel for all of this. Without it, there’s no way to know if you’re improving or just spinning your wheels. That’s why superforecasters actively look for feedback and treat mistakes as stepping stones, not embarrassments.
For instance, imagine a forecasting tournament where people are asked to predict global events. A superforecaster might notice they’re consistently too optimistic. By digging into the data, they realize they’ve underestimated the chances of negative outcomes. Once they spot this trend, they tweak their approach—and suddenly, their predictions get a whole lot closer to reality.
This cycle—predict, get feedback, revise—creates a kind of virtuous loop. Every round of learning makes their judgment a bit sharper, helping them tune in to what really matters and tune out all the noise.
So, here’s the key takeaway: Humility isn’t a weakness—it’s a superpower. Being willing to admit mistakes, question your assumptions, and change your mind when the evidence changes, that’s what separates the best forecasters from the rest.
In a world where the future is always uncertain, the ability to adapt is your ultimate advantage.
